text: I think 4 guys have a legitimate case being Wilt, KAJ, Jordan, and LeBron. Greatest player, imo, shouldn't have rings as an important metric. Isiah Thomas isn't greater than Nash although the latter never got past the conference finals. Each of these four were the most dominant forces of their eras. They had to literally change the rules because Wilt was too good. In modern basketball Wilt would still be one of if not the most athletic player in the league. His skillset translates to any era and few guys all time could slow him down. Perhaps this says more about the league in the 60s but Wilt has many records that will never come close to falling. Kareem has the longest streak of dominance of any player, has the most points and MVPs, and was the best offensive and defensive threat in the league simultaneously at his peak. MJ transcended basketball with his play style and will to dominate. Like KAJ he was the best offensive player of his time while being a top defender and arguably the best perimeter defender ever. You could argue he should've had about 8 MVPs and I wouldn't disagree. LeBron is the best all around player I think we've seen. Maybe he has an advantage being able to look back on more greatness than the others but the level of talent is undeniable. He can guard 1-5, has arguably a top 5 court court vision all time, can make passes no one else can, and is faster and stronger than anyone we've seen at his size. In terms of dominant longevity he's only behind KAJ and should surpass him barring serious injury or an extended lockout. Excluding the 2011 finals Bron has an incredible playoff track record and has led some of the greatest carry jobs in NBA history. You could argue Bron should have a couple more MVPs like Jordan and again I wouldn't disagree. He also got robbed of at least one DPOY imo during his time in Miami. Shaq has an argument for most dominant player ever at his peak along with Wilt. I think the length of his dominance puts him behind the other 4 but definitely in the top 10. Magic/Bird are other guys that you could argue but again I think they're slightly behind the others in terms of overall dominance (perhaps somewhat due to coming into the league together and competing against one another) and their later years being taken away by HIV and injury, respectively.

text: I use a very arbitrary judgement. After a decade, longevity doesn't mean anything to me. I of course would never value a 3 year career as a GOAT candidate, but when guys are 10, 12, 13, 15, seasons in, hitting 20 doesn't factor in at all. I get people who like to use it, and people who don't (like me). One of my go to's for anti-longevity is Karl Malone has never been considered a better scorer than MJ, with significantly more points. Ditto for Kareem. Jason Kidd is also never viewed as a better shooter than Peja Stojakovic even with more total made 3s. I value it, but after the more than a decade mark, I toss it out. Others may weight it more heavily. Peak factors in greatly, but it can't be too short. Perfect case is MJ vs Shaq. Both have to me, the 2 highest peaks in the modern era ever. Shaq's was much shorter than MJ though so while I love using peak, length of it usually comes into play, but I still value the intensity of it more than a total length being the defining factor. I factor in skills, winning, domination over your peers, being the 1st option/second option, did you make your teammates better and help them grow vs blockbuster trades/Free agency?, Peak, per game rates, efficiency, volume, two way player? I factor in a lot. Some times things can weigh more in one case but not another. Greatness is very subjective.
label: analysis

text: I'd say there are only two serious candidates and we all know which two I'm talking about. It can't possibly be anyone before Jordan because the concept of "GOAT" was invented to elevate Jordan above those who came before him. There were rivalries between Bird and Magic, Russell and Chamberlain, and obviously debates between them, but nobody talked about "greatest of all time" before Jordan. Starting in the late 90 and into the 00's there's a consensus on Jordan, which very strongly implies that he surpassed the players before him while no one came close to surpassing him for quite some time. In fact the narrative during that period wasn't whether anyone would ever surpass Jordan but rather whether there would be "the next Jordan". Kobe Bryant was probably the best direct replica but in his prime, nobody seriously thought he was better than the original. Some of this also spilled over into the early perceptions of LeBron James. LeBron has meanwhile cemented himself firmly in the status of "greatest since Jordan" at the bare minimum. He was good enough that we all shut up about "the next Jordan" because we were satisfied with the first LeBron. And watching LeBron throughout his career does make it hard to imagine anyone being an even greater player. Now that LeBron has managed to open the debate, there are a ton of people wading in with respect for the pre-Jordan era as well. And I think that era deserves some respect, though of everyone from that era the only one I think might approach MJ's greatness was Bill Russell. But ultimately, there was no question about it being anyone other than Jordan until LeBron came around, which is what makes LeBron the only true contender.
